text: Cassini was sent to Saturn mostly to study the rings and the moons, but NASA chose a slow plunge into Saturn near the end instead of landing on a moon. A landed or crashed probe could carry Earth microbes, or leave debris on a moon. Saturn's upper air would tear Cassini to pieces and mostly vaporize it, like a meteor. Thats the contamination worry, especially if it hit a moon that might have an ocean under the surface. It also ran low on fuel, and the crash gave one last close look at the rings before the end.

The leg that you plant to push is taking way more impact than you might think. You're not just balancing, you're also loading that knee and ankle with every push, then suddenly changing direction or leaning back while the board moves under you. That mix of impact, torsion, and balance work tends to irritate the standing leg.

Most people assume the pain is from the motion of riding, but it's usually just that one spot getting overworked. If the board is too big or too small, your foot position shifts constantly to maintain balance, which means you might be landing in awkward angles. Check your setup first.

The knee is the usual suspect here. The meniscus or the joint capsule can take the pounding from repeated landings. A lot of skaters start feeling "it hurts when I ride" after days of pushing off the same leg, especially after a big impact like going down a steep ramp.

One practical fix is to alternate which leg pushes when possible. You can't always, but consciously switching the push-off leg reduces chronic stress. Also, make sure you're actually wearing sneakers with real support and aren't riding in flip-flops or soft soles.

Don't skip stretching the standing hip and ankle before you ride. A few minutes of gentle flexion and extension helps you absorb impact better. If the pain feels sharp or you're limping, back off before it turns into a real problem.

Most importantly, if this persists, see a sports physio. They can tell you whether it's the knee or the joint capsule. It's worth the appointment, don't rely on feeling it out at the skatepark.

i think people get tripped up because the word sounds like a place they were born in. But it's more a marker of ancestral connection, not current residence. Most black Americans grew up in the US, maybe their whole life, yet their families came from West and Central Africa centuries ago. That connection runs through generations, so the label is about lineage, not a recent plane ride. It also helps describe a shared cultural history and identity. The US has a complex Black experience, with roots in many communities and regions. Calling people Afro-American doesn't mean their grandkids are from Lagos or Accra. It just traces the line back to African peoples. So the term is broad, and not every person will identify with it, but it exists as one way to name that heritage. You might also wonder why not just American, well, the racial grouping adds a historical layer. It's not trying to turn every Black American into an immigrant or expat. The continent comes up in the family tree, not the mailing address. Even if no one in that family has visited Africa for generations, the label still makes sense as a cultural and historical category.

they mostly get guns from local black markets, captured enemy depots and old army stockpiles, and sometimes from allies and outside actors. Why keep getting them when the war has barely wound down? Well, not at all, in practice. Hezbollah and Russian supplies helped shape the balance, but local militias still wanted arms to hold territory and fight off rival groups. Even the state kept pulling weapons from storage because new front lines formed, and demand from fighters stayed high. New recruits kept showing up, which made buying ammo and guns continue. Smuggling through borders kept flowing, so supply stayed easier than most people expect.

i keep saying to people that all drugs are toxic, and i only half agree. There are drugs with relatively low side effects. Caffeine is a drug, and for most people it doesn't feel like a crash if you're not overdoing it (well, mostly). The issue with heroine, coke and that whole party, is that the pleasure they give is so strong it pulls your brain's reward system around by the collar. Your brain is wired for small everyday rewards, like getting a snack from the fridge or a text back. A drug that spikes dopamine way beyond that normal range doesn't sit quietly. Your system notices the imbalance and starts defending itself, that's tolerance. So a drug that makes you feel euphoric also teaches your brain to want the feeling again. That's an adverse effect even if you're not sick. You get used to the high and need more to get the same kick, and that's the start of dependence.

a zero side effect strong pleasure drug would still have to touch more than the pleasure center. Nothing works on one little thing. If it raises the reward signal it also changes how the brain predicts and craves. In plain terms, the more amazing a feeling is, the harder it is to stop wanting it. That's why the strongest pleasurable drugs tend to be the ones people cant let go of. You can design a substance that feels nice without wrecking your liver or lungs, sure. But if a designer goes for intense pleasure and zero adverse effects, they're missing the point, because the wanting more is the effect.

That's what gets left out when people blame all drugs. The word drug doesn't mean poison, it means a substance that changes how the body or mind works. Caffeine changes you a little. Some meds make you feel better without wrecking you. The bad rep comes from the ones that make the biggest changes, where the payoff is large enough that your nervous system has to recalibrate. Once you need to recalibrate you've lost the ability to feel normal pleasure the same way, even if you're not physically ill. So a mild drug with low adverse effects can exist, but a drug with intense pleasure and zero consequences is the odd one out. The brain's response to the intense feeling is itself a consequence, so the more pleasure it gives, the more the body fights it.

A long shopping day means walking, turning, squatting, carrying bags and standing for hours, and your legs, feet and lower back absorb it all. If the floors are hard, its hot, or you've just been sitting around before, your body starts feeling wrecked. You're not imagining this. Ha, that's funny. I think your brother was running a little attention trick on you. You had just been saying silk five times and spelling it, so your brain was stuck in that fast tongue exercise. Then he throws the cow question at you, and a cow makes milk the obvious connected word. It's not that you forgot the answer. The repetition, plus the strong cow and milk link, made the wrong answer feel fine. That little slip also fits the kind of thing those quick tongue tests are meant to show: the mind can get carried away by a strong related idea when attention shifts suddenly. You didn't get it wrong on purpose. The cue was too strong, and you were already talking fast. His point was probably to catch you off guard. I bet he had this reaction in mind, maybe just to watch you blink.

Hi,
I get the mix of questions, because buying a house feels like a lot of moving parts at once. The thing people miss is that the purchase price is only the start. A mortgage can look affordable one month and not the next if rates change. Insurance, council tax, heating and repairs are the hidden drag. I’d make sure you have room in the budget for the things that never stop, dont only look at the deposit. Get the property inspected by someone neutral and ask about leaks, wiring, drainage or weird renovations. Walk through every room, open cupboards, check for damp patches. A house doesnt come with a warranty once the deal is done, so finding the bad news early saves pain. Check the street and neighbours, because you’re buying a place to live. Don’t rush viewings just because another buyer is interested. If you’ve got a mortgage quote in writing that’s fine, but don’t rely on a promise. Take your time, get the paperwork checked, and remember you can walk away before completion if something looks off. The worst mistake is falling for the house and skipping the boring checks. That’s when little details cost a lot later.

Honestly, there's almost no difference. Those 3-in-1 products really just use the same base formula across their whole range, so a person can pick a scent rather than a special treatment type. It's not that a product does everything, but that it does the one shared job.

A shampoo is built to clean and lift oils and dead skin from your scalp. A conditioner is built to deposit stuff onto your hair. The 3-in-1 just mixes the same ingredients together, and that combination is fine for average hair, but if your scalp needs an exfoliating scrub or your hair needs a protein repair, the 3-in-1 can leave a thin coat behind. Some of these all-in-ones have a higher surfactant blend that can leave strands frizzy or dull. A person doesn't need to worry if their hair is fine, but they might notice it.

Hi,
The question makes sense people think a moving continent is way too slow to notice. The practical answer is GPS. Researchers run GPS receivers at fixed survey points on the land and record where those points sit. Satellites help them get millimetre level position then they compare readings weeks months or years apart. If a spot shifts a centimetre over a couple of years they divide the distance by that time to get mm/year. i think that is where my head starts spinning but its the way they do it. Most tectonic spots we monitor creep at the scale of a centimetre or a few centimetres every year slow as nail growth but persistent. Its easy to picture if you think about it. A few cm a year times a million years becomes tens of kilometres. That is the big drift we can see from repeated GPS positions.
The catch is noise. Seasons groundwater changes tides and local ground settling can mimic movement so they need many stations and filter the small effects. One point alone can be fooled. Different parts of a continent also move differently and the tectonic piece can flex a bit. For the friend asking stable GPS data from lots of stations is the real method.

inbreeding means two related people have a kid. If parents share ancestry they usually share copies of rare harmful genes. Many of those genes stay hidden when there's just one copy, but if both parents pass the same bad copy the child can show the problem. That matters because genes influence how sharp and curious someone is, while environment does too.

Related parents share more of the same genes, so bad copies are more likely to land together. Its like a car with one faulty part. With only one the engine can be fine, but with two the engine breaks. In practice, the drop in average IQ is mainly about paired-up bad genes becoming active, plus smaller health effects that make learning and brain wiring more difficult. And the risk climbs with how close the relatives are, since closer relatives share more of the same genes.

i think of it like slapping your face versus your upper arm; the face sting lasts much longer because the brain has a bigger sensory region for that area. It's not that the arm is special, it's just the brain and tissue together making it seem milder. Also the arm skin is thicker, and the shoulder has muscle and fat to cushion impacts. So a hit, stab or bullet in the arm may not penetrate as badly, which changes how painful it feels.

Here is what makes them so different in your body. Carbon monoxide doesn't make your nose or throat react, it steals the oxygen slot from your red blood cells. Your blood carries oxygen using a little protein called hemoglobin, and carbon monoxide is a much stronger stick-it than oxygen. Once it holds on, the whole cell is busy with this other chemical and can't deliver oxygen to your muscles and brain. Your brain uses oxygen to keep you calm and thinking, so if it runs out you get headache, dizziness, and confusion, and that is not something you can feel easily. That is the trap. Think of it as someone locking the doors while telling the building it is already full of air.

Carbon dioxide is the opposite, it's a by-product the lungs can remove quickly. It's also the chemical that tells your kidneys how to keep the blood balanced, so it's part of the body's self-balancing system. If there's too much carbon dioxide you gasp, it wakes you up, so it's not invisible the way carbon monoxide is. Carbon monoxide, by contrast, can build up quietly while you sleep. Car engines and heating systems are common sources, and because the gas is colorless and odorless you don't necessarily wake up or notice. That's why the poison part is mostly about oxygen transport, not about being chemically mean.

Your doctor might give oxygen through a mask or even put you in a special high-pressure chamber in serious cases. A little monoxide can be cleared naturally once you get fresh air, but a lot of it locks up your blood supply and leaves the tissues starving, and prevention is always easier. You don't need any background to see why the two gases behave so differently from each other.

The brace position isn't used for every emergency, it's what you do when a hard landing or impact is likely. The idea is to put bones and muscles between you and the cabin, so your body stops getting slammed around. You sit up and pull your knees toward your chest, holding the seat in front of you. That compact ball puts your limbs between you and the impact. If the plane hits something or slams down, it's much worse when your neck or head takes the force while you're spread out. A passenger flying with loose limbs is much more likely to bang their head or chest; bracing spreads the load and keeps major parts from swinging around.

Well, mostly this one is like a tiny controlled bump before the real one. Your arms and legs act as the shock absorbers, and your seatbelt plus grip keeps you in place. It doesnt make every hard landing safe, but it reduces how far your body moves or hits the surrounding cabin. If the crew tells you to brace, do it instead of lying flat or staring out the window, because the position shapes how your body travels when the plane stops suddenly.

Most pre-industrial businesses were small workshops, guild operations, or family trades. They served nearby towns, not entire markets, so they rarely built the kind of scale that keeps a brand alive for centuries. Well-known names survive when the business keeps operating, not just once existed. Its hard to remember a shop that only served its street, and fame sticks when people see a name everywhere. Before machines, growth depended on hands and local customers, not mass distribution. Industrialization changed production methods, distribution, and ownership, so many older forms of trading just faded out or got absorbed. The names we actually know today are the rare exceptions that made it through.

The reason a bank can be cheaper even when the dealership posts a lower rate is that the rate is only the label, not the bill. I kept looking at the APR and got it wrong. The dealer had the pretty number, but it was tied to a much larger financed amount and a longer term, and they stuffed add-ons into the loan. When I pulled the same cash price and compared total paid over the whole loan, the bank came out under it.

I tried this after shopping for a new car and getting a financing offer that sounded too good to be true. The dealer quoted 5.0% while my bank was 7.2%. That looked like a free lunch. The catch was the loan setup. The dealer's quote rolled in optional protection, a slightly higher out-the-door amount, and a longer repayment window. My bank quote used a lower principal and a shorter term. On paper the bank's higher rate made me nervous, but the math was more persuasive. Using numbers I could stand behind: a $31,000 bank loan at 7.2% for 48 months cost roughly $4,800 in interest, or about $35,800 in total payments. The dealer option was a lower rate, but the $33,450 amount with add-ons over 60 months came out near $37,900 in total. The lower rate did not save me anything.

A low dealer APR is often a trap. It can look cheap per dollar while you are borrowing more, paying more months, and covering fees the bank would not charge you. The total cost of money is what matters. I have seen friends buy optional packages because they were attached to the financing, then wonder why the payment was higher. The bank avoided that stacking. That is the difference people miss. The advertised rate can look better, but it wins only if the amount, term, and fees are the same. When they are not, the higher-rate bank loan can still leave less money spent.

I am not a car-finance expert, but that comparison is why I would not trust a low dealer rate until I got the total loan amount, the term, and the fees in writing. A nice APR can still be the expensive choice. The dealer may be right about the rate, but the rest of the paper changes the answer, and that change is what makes the bank option cheaper in the end.

I get why people want a single national rule about marijuana, but I keep coming back to a simpler idea: states should be allowed to decide for themselves. In California, adults can buy it from licensed retailers, while in some states a small stash is still enough for police to search you. That split isn't chaos; it's experimentation with tax rates, packaging, and who can sell. I prefer letting states experiment, the way they did with same-sex marriage. The feds used to raid state dispensaries, but now they mostly give states breathing room. That room matters when a county lets a grower license operate near a school, or when a state caps store openings near a highway. More states legalizing means a real patchwork, and a patchwork works if the federal government stops treating every state law like a violation. I'd rather have states argue about where to put dispensaries than force one rule on fifty.

Our bodies don’t make electricity like a wall socket does. Its more like a big salty plumbing system running through everything you are, with cells pushing little charged particles around. Your nerves fire when sodium and potassium shift, creating that tiny zap you feel in your legs, or whatever, a muscle twitch. The heart isn’t a generator, its just the muscle cells in its walls letting ion channels open and close, which sets up the wave that makes it beat.

When i first got serious about making beats, i spent an entire summer hunting through used record stores for anything with a good groove you could loop. The old 45s and 12 inch pressings were where the magic was hidden, dusty crates full of soul, funk, and old gospel. You'd grab a record, find a four bar break with no melody in the way, and drop it on the sampler. Most of the time its just a slice of drums or a bassline you stretch across your whole track.

That part is the thing people usually get wrong. A sample is not this huge chunk of a song pasted in. Its more like chopping a banana into slices then rearranging them in a different order, or turning a little drumbreak loop into a whole rhythm section. You pull out the snare hit from the middle of the record, loop it, bend the pitch down to match your key, then build the rest of the track around it. The old records matter because their grooves feel human. The drummer wasnt quantized or grid locked the way modern DAWs can be, so the timing has real swing to it, and that is what you are trying to keep.

How does a musician actually do it technically? Well, mostly it works like this: you get the file into your sampler or DAW, mark in points and out points, adjust the length, then layer on top with your own drums, synths, and vocals. You have to be careful not to over stretch, because looping a snare too slow makes it sound like mud. But if you nudge the pitch or add reverb, the old groove fits right into a new track. Sometimes you find a short vocal chop and turn that into a melody, or lift a single chord from an old piano riff. The trick is keeping it recognizable without letting the original own the new song.

My favorite trick was taking a 12 inch breakbeat, isolating the drums, then running it through a lofi filter. That made it feel aged and warm instead of clean and sterile. A lot of hip-hop producers from the 90s made whole hits this way, and it still works today. You don't need a perfect recording to make a good beat. You just need a moment in an old record that has enough character to loop and hang a new song on.

My head hurts because my skull isn't just a bony box, it's wrapped in this weird mesh of nerves and blood vessels that react violently to almost nothing. i used to think headaches were just pressure building up, but it's really more like a bad alarm system. The trigeminal nerve acts like a smoke detector, going off when youre stressed, dehydrated, and blood vessels dilate. 

It feels like a tight band squeezing your temples, or a crushing pressure right behind the eyes. The brain literally amplifies the signal when youre tired, turning a mild twitch in those vessels into this severe pain. 

You cant exactly point to a specific painful spot because the receptors are mostly in the outer meninges. i find it weird how a tiny drop of caffeine can shift the whole sensation, proving a headache isn't triggered by one single physical thing. I needed water and sleep.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m., and surprisingly there was no line at all. Two people came out to about $130, which felt pretty steep. Before going, I figured the price would be comparable to a steakhouse. Afterward, I learned the buffet actually cost somewhat more than what I had expected to pay at one.

I was disappointed that steak wasn’t offered. At that price, I assumed there would be some kind of steak option. The meat choices included lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but those are things I feel like you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn’t run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. The problem was there were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I didn’t want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station didn’t seem especially distinctive either. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I didn’t try any.

Overall, I’d call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you’re curious, it’s worth trying once, especially if there’s no wait. But if the line is long, I’d probably reconsider.

★★★★☆ Keeping it

The space bar rattles. Hit it with the edge of your thumb and it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key repeats now and then, so "example" becomes "eexample" and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I'm typing fast and not looking.

I paid $38 and kept it anyway, because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I had already pulled off a keycap and found out for myself: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don't ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle.

Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I'd have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now, actually.

About two years ago we called Rockmount Ranch Wear and ordered two shirts for my dad. They never came because the sales rep got the delivery address wrong. Her handwritten 7 was read as a 1. The address was supposed to be 5407, but the package was sent to 5401. The residents at 5401 took it to the local UPS store to send it back. The package then disappeared and was never seen or heard from again. We didn't learn of this until several weeks later. During the dispute we also ordered two more shirts. Rockmount refused to refund the original two. The owner took over, admitted the shipment went to the wrong address, but said no refund until the shirts were returned. He claimed we were partly at fault because we weren't friendly enough with the residents at 5401, four doors away. We did dispute the original charge with our credit-card company and we eventually got a credit back.
